claims.text: A hybrid variance-descriptor, random-forest, and phase-field methodology can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness of HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately and efficiently than first-principles/CALPHAD approaches.
The reported HfNbTiVAl10 state is a hierarchical heterostructure produced by arc melting and thermomechanical processing.
Variance in atomic planar density, ionization energy, and the D parameter can serve as descriptors of alloy heterogeneity.
Variance descriptors can be fed into a random-forest model and fused with phase-field tensile and fracture simulations.
The methodology is intended for room-temperature tensile and fracture testing of samples made by consistent homogenization, cold-rolling, recrystallization, and aging protocols.
Hierarchical microstructural heterogeneity and multiscale chemical fluctuations mediate local stress distributions and damage initiation.
The proposed variance descriptors capture the effects of the heterogeneity on local stress and damage initiation.
Local property fluctuations affect dislocation behavior and elastic mismatch.
Representing these fluctuations allows more accurate modeling of stress–strain response and fracture initiation with phase-field simulations.
An ensemble tree model can correlate material features with macroscopic elastic properties.
The integrated model can bypass computationally demanding full ab initio or CALPHAD evaluations.
The hybrid method will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–20% relative to traditional methods.
The hybrid method will reduce computational time by up to 50% relative to traditional methods.
Composition-only machine-learning methods do not account for hierarchical microstructural variance.
Reliability may decrease when actual microstructural fluctuations differ significantly from those assumed by the model.
Reliability may decrease when an unmodeled fracture mechanism, such as transformation-induced plasticity, dominates behavior.
The numerical accuracy and efficiency gains depend on microstructure-data quality, resolution, and processing history.
A blinded comparison against first-principles/CALPHAD predictions, followed by tensile and fracture measurements, can prospectively test the method.
The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid method fails to reduce prediction error by at least 15% and computational time by 50%, or if any predicted property has more than 20% error.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome promises computational-time savings of 'up to 50%,' whereas the falsification rule requires at least a 50% reduction. An upper-bound expectation does not coherently support a minimum 50% pass threshold.
